Group: Security Dashboard
Item: Security Dashboard Details Page
Guidance: Monitor your cluster security posture in a single customizable view. Security Dashboard is a customizable and dynamic console that provides a unified view of your Nutanix infrastructure's security. By default, the Security Dashboard displays the following information widgets: ¶ Summary on page 85 STIG Policy on page 86 Security Hardening on page 86 Vulnerabilities on page 93 System Account Passwords on page 93 Use the View menu on the dashboard to switch between different cluster views. The widget data updates dynamically based on the following options: ¶ All clusters Individual cluster Selection of clusters ¶ Note: If the Security Dashboard in the Prism Central VM restarts, active tasks in the Security Dashboard are marked as canceled. If this occurs, review the associated subtasks for details about incomplete operations. ¶ Summary The Summary widget allows you to view your open security issues or focus on the clusters that have the most number of security issues. You can click the Summary pie graph to view the following information. ¶ Total number of issues in the clusters Number of issues in the clusters categorized based on the following issue categories: ¶ Security Hardening STIG Issues Vulnerabilities Local Account Passwords ¶ Tip: The Security Dashboard refreshes once daily. Updating the STIG check based vulnerabilities information requires a manual refresh. You can initiate a manual refresh by clicking the refresh icon at the bottom of the widget. Manual refresh process takes some approximately 20 minutes to 2 hours to complete and depends on the number of clusters in your environment. ¶ STIG Policy ¶ STIG helps detect deviation from the security baseline configuration of the operating system and hypervisor to remain in compliance. Nutanix has implemented the Controller VM to support STIG compliance with the RHEL 9 STIG as published by DISA. For more information, see Security Dashboard STIG Guidance Reference. ¶ The STIG Policy widget provides an accurate snapshot of policy violations or deviations (resulting in failure) from the baseline STIG policy. This widget displays the STIG policy compliance status according to controls and resources. ¶ Note: The STIG checks are run only on the node running primary Prism Element. ¶ Status by Controls (Unique) Number of unique STIG controls that are not met. Status by Resources (Total) Total number of individual resources that have failed a set of STIG controls. ¶ Click View Failed Controls to view the list of STIG controls that are not met. ¶ STIG Policy - Failed Controls ¶ The STIG Policy -Failed Controls dialog box allows you to view STIG controls that do not meet the required settings. ¶ Security Hardening ¶ Use the Security Hardening widget to view the status of security hardening controls that are applied to your clusters and to configure multiple security hardening controls directly. ¶ The Security Hardening widget includes the following security hardening configurations: ¶ Security Profiles Apply a predefined security posture to each cluster by selecting one of the Standard, Elevated, or Strict profiles. Selecting a new profile starts a rolling reboot of all nodes. For more information, see Security Profiles on page 87 and Configuring Security Profiles on page 87. ¶ Cluster Lockdown Enables Cluster Lockdown mode to restrict administrative access and enhance security. For more information, see Configuring Cluster Lockdown using Security Dashboard on page 93. ¶ Defense Consent Banner Enables Defense Consent Banner. Once enabled, the system displays the consent banner of the US Department of Defense when connecting with SSH. You must set the Defense Consent Banner individually for Controller VM and AHV hosts. ¶ Host Secure Boot Enables Host Secure Boot to prevent unauthorized firmware or software from running on AHV or ESXi hosts during the boot process. Host secure boot is a unified extensible firmware interface (UEFI) firmware feature that ensures only trusted system components are allowed to run at startup. For more information on enabling and verifying host secure boot, see Host Secure Boot (UEFI). ¶ Network Segmentation Shows the network segmentation status for each cluster. The network segmentation isolates CVM traffic types on separate VLANs or physical networks to improve security and performance. Configure network ¶ segmentation from the network configuration settings page in Prism Element. For more information, see Securing Traffic Through Network Segmentation on page 182. Log Forwarding Shows the log forwarding status for each cluster. Log forwarding sends CVM system, audit, AIDE, and SCMA logs to a central log host to preserve log integrity and meet compliance requirements. Configure log forwarding from the network configuration settings page in Prism Element. For more information, see Log Forwarding on page 170. You can also configure security hardening setting using the nCLI interface. For more information, see Hardening Instructions Using nCLI on page 174. ¶ Security Profiles Use security profiles to simplify cluster security configuration by selecting a predefined profile in the Security dashboard. Security profiles bundle hardening settings into predefined tiers so that cluster administrators can set a security posture with a single profile selection instead of configuring many individual settings. Security profiles are available in the Security dashboard and apply to AOS and AHV clusters. The feature includes the following tiers: ¶ Standard: Represents the default recommended security posture with baseline protections and minimal performance impact. ¶ Elevated: Tightens authentication and kernel protections compared to Standard, including additional CPU mitigations and higher performance overhead. ¶ Strict: Applies the highest hardening level for high-security requirements, including stricter controls and the highest performance impact. ¶ Security profile selection changes multiple hardening settings together. For detailed profile-to-setting values, see Security Profile to Hardening Settings Mapping on page 88. The following behavior and scope apply to security profile selection: ¶ Security profile updates apply only to AHV hosts. If a cluster contains AHV hosts, all AHV hosts in the cluster must run AHV 11.2 or later. The security profile does not update non-AHV hosts in mixed-hypervisor clusters. ¶ Updating the security profile on a cluster with more than three nodes starts a rolling reboot of all nodes. ¶ In mixed-hypervir clusters, the security profile applies only to AOS and AHV nodes. ¶ When you upgrade from an earlier AOS version to the version that supports security profiles (AOS 7.6), the profile can initially appear as Not_Set. You can change from Not_Set to one of the profile options. ¶ If the cluster is not registered to Prism Central, use the Prism Element workflow to set the security profile. For more information, see Configuring Security Profiles Using Prism Element on page 171. ¶ Note: If the Security Dashboard in the Prism Central VM restarts, active tasks in the Security Dashboard are marked as canceled. If this occurs, review the associated subtasks for details about incomplete operations. ¶ Configuring Security Profiles ¶ Set a predefined tier of hardening settings on a cluster by choosing a security profile in the Security dashboard. ¶ Before you begin Ensure that you meet the following requirements: ¶ Prism Central is on version pc.7.6 or later. The cluster runs AOS 7.6 or later. All AHV hosts run AHV 11.2 or later. The cluster is healthy and no critical operations are running. ¶ About this task To set the security profile for a cluster from the Security dashboard in Prism Central, follow these steps: ¶ Note: Setting a new profile starts a rolling reboot of all nodes in the cluster. For clusters with fewer than three nodes, reboot the hosts manually after the profile is set. ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. Log in to Prism Central as an administrator. ¶ 2. From the Application Switcher Function, select the Infrastructure application and from the navigation bar, ¶ select Network & Security > Security Dashboard. ¶ 3. In the Hardening widget, click Configure under Security Profiles. ¶ 4. On the Security Profiles page, click Manage for the target cluster. ¶ 5. In the Manage Security Profile dialog box, select one of the following profiles: ¶ » Standard: Baseline protections with minimal performance impact. » Elevated: Additional authentication and kernel protections with higher performance impact. » Strict: Highest hardening level with the highest performance impact. For the per-tier hardening setting values, see Security Profile to Hardening Settings Mapping on page 88. ¶ 6. Select the acknowledgment checkbox. The checkbox text depends on the cluster size: ¶ For clusters with three or more nodes, the checkbox reads I am aware that a rolling reboot of hosts will start once a new profile is set. ¶ For clusters with fewer than three nodes, the checkbox reads I will manually reboot the hosts once a new profile is set. ¶ 7. Click Set Profile. The system starts applying the selected profile to the cluster. ¶ Security Profile to Hardening Settings Mapping Compare how the Standard, Elevated, and Strict security profiles map to AOS and AHV security hardening settings. The following tables list the profile-based hardening configuration values for AOS and AHV. For the description of each hardening setting listed in this mapping, see Security Profile Hardening Settings Reference on page 90. ¶ Security Profile Summary ¶ Standard - baseline security profile with core protections; minimal performance impact ¶ Elevated - tightens authentication and kernel protections beyond Standard; higher performance overhead than Standard ¶ Strict - maximum hardening profile for high-security requirements; highest performance impact among the three profiles ¶ AOS Security Setting Standard Elevated Strict cluster-scma-schedule Weekly Daily Daily high-strength-password off on on aide off off on max-login-attempt 5 3 3 lockout-sec 900 900 0 userspace-core on on off banner off off on ¶ In the AOS security settings, a lockout-sec value of 0 represents no unlock. AOS kernel security settings require a reboot to apply. ¶ AOS Kernel Security Standard Elevated Strict Setting kernel-core/logcore on on off slub-debug off off on page-poison off off on init-on-free off off on kernel-mitigations off on on processor-mitigations off on on ¶ AHV Security Setting Standard Elevated Strict high-strength-password off on on auto-unlock on off off kernel-security-profile standard elevated strict ¶ AHV Security Setting Standard Elevated Strict aide off off on banner Not set Not set on userspace-core log log off kernel-core on on off ¶ The following notes apply to the AHV security settings: ¶ The auto-unlock setting is implicitly bound to the high-strength-password policy behavior. The banner text is controlled by AOS. AHV kernel security settings require a reboot to apply. ¶ AHV Kernel Security Standard Elevated Strict Setting gdsmitigation on on on srsomitigation off on on forcepti off on on memorypoison off off on slub_debug off off on retbleedmitigation off on on itlbmultihitmitigation off on on ¶ In the AHV kernel security settings, slub_debug is configured through the memorypoison setting. ¶ Security Profile Hardening Settings Reference ¶ Review each security profile hardening setting and where it applies. The settings listed here are the hardening controls that security profiles bundle into the Standard, Elevated, and Strict tiers. For the tier-by-tier value assigned to each setting, see Security Profile to Hardening Settings Mapping on page 88. ¶ Setting definitions aide The advanced intrusion detection environment (AIDE) setting is a file and directory integrity checker. This setting applies to the CVM, PCVM, and AHV host. banner The banner setting displays a banner message when a user logs in over SSH. This setting applies to the CVM, PCVM, and AHV host. ¶ cluster-scma-schedule The SCMA schedule sets how often the security configuration management automation (SCMA) framework runs hardening compliance checks across the cluster. Allowed values are Daily and Weekly. A more frequent schedule detects configuration drift sooner at the cost of additional cluster activity. This setting applies to AOS on the CVM. ¶ forcepti (AHV) The forcepti setting enforces unconditional page table isolation (PTI) to protect against Meltdown by completely separating user-space and kernel-space memory maps. This setting applies to the AHV kernel. ¶ gdsmitigation (AHV) The GDS mitigation addresses the gather data sampling (Downfall) hardware vulnerability by restricting unprivileged speculative access to stale vector register data. This setting applies to the AHV kernel. ¶ high-strength-password The high strength password setting enforces stronger password policies on the CVM, PCVM, or AHV host. This setting enforces the following requirements: ¶ A minimum password length of 16 characters (minlen=16) At least 8 characters that differ from the old password (difok=8) A maximum of 4 consecutive characters from the same character class (maxclassrepeat=4) A check against a user-specific list of prohibited passwords (dictcheck=1) This setting applies to the CVM, PCVM, and AHV host. init-on-free The init_on_free setting is a Linux kernel boot parameter that enhances memory security by automatically zeroing (wiping) memory pages and heap objects immediately after they are freed. This setting applies to the CVM and PCVM. itlbmultihitmitigation The iTLB multihit mitigation addresses the iTLB multihit vulnerability (CVE-2018-12207) by restricting KVM guests from executing large pages, which prevents malicious VMs from inducing host machine check exceptions. This setting applies to the AHV kernel. kernel-core The kernel core dump is a snapshot of the kernel's memory at the time of a crash. Enabling kernel core captures a core dump if the kernel crashes, which helps you debug kernel-related issues. This setting applies to the CVM, PCVM, and AHV host. kernel-mitigations The kernel mitigations setting enables OS-level software defenses within the Linux kernel to protect against side-channel attacks and memory corruption exploits. This setting applies to the CVM and PCVM. ¶ lockout-sec The lockout duration sets how long, in seconds, an account remains locked after exceeding the maximum failed login attempts (max-login-attempt). A value of 0 means the account does not unlock automatically and requires administrator intervention. This setting applies to AOS on the CVM. ¶ max-login-attempt The maximum login attempts setting controls how many consecutive failed login attempts are allowed before the account is locked. Lower values reduce the window for brute-force attacks at the cost of more frequent lockouts from typos. This setting applies to AOS on the CVM. ¶ memorypoison The memory poison setting enables page poisoning and SLUB/SLAB debugging to overwrite freed memory pages with a pattern, preventing use-after-free exploits and detecting memory corruption. This setting applies to the AHV kernel. The equivalent controls on AOS are exposed as page-poison and slub-debug. ¶ min-password-length The minimum password length setting sets the smallest number of characters a user password must contain. Higher values produce stronger passwords at the cost of user convenience. This setting applies to AOS on the CVM. ¶ page-poison The page poison setting overwrites freed memory pages with a specific value to help detect use-after-free vulnerabilities. Enabling page poison helps prevent use-after-free attacks but might reduce performance. This setting applies to the CVM and PCVM. The equivalent control on AHV is memorypoison. ¶ processor-mitigations The processor mitigation setting enables mitigations against processor-based vulnerabilities. Enabling processor mitigation protects against certain types of attacks but might reduce performance. This setting applies to the CVM and PCVM. ¶ retbleedmitigation The Retbleed mitigation addresses the Retbleed vulnerability (CVE-2022-29900, CVE-2022-29901), a speculative-execution vulnerability affecting processors that use return instructions. Enabling the mitigation protects against these attacks by restricting the use of indirect branches and returns, which might reduce performance depending on the workload. This setting applies to the AHV kernel. ¶ slub-debug The slub debug setting is a memory debugging technique that can help detect memory corruption issues. Enabling slub debug mitigation helps prevent memory corruption but might reduce performance. This setting applies to the CVM, PCVM, and the AHV kernel. On AHV, slub_debug is configured through the memorypoison setting. ¶ srsomitigation (AHV) The SRSO mitigation addresses the speculative return stack overflow vulnerability on AMD CPUs by strictly controlling speculation of return instructions. This setting applies to the AHV kernel. ¶ userspace-core The user-space core dump setting controls whether the operating system records the working memory of a user-space program when it crashes or terminates abnormally. Core dumps assist in diagnosing or debugging errors, but Nutanix recommends keeping them disabled in production to prevent stack traces that might contain sensitive data. This setting applies to the CVM, PCVM, and AHV host. ¶ Note: Do not set userspace-core to on unless instructed by Nutanix Support, to ensure data privacy. ¶ Configuring Cluster Lockdown using Security Dashboard You can configure cluster lockdown directly using the Security Dashboard. ¶ About this task To configure cluster lockdown using the Security Dashboard, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. Log in to Prism Central as an administrator. ¶ 2. From the Application Switcher Function, select the Admin Center application. ¶ 3. From the navigation bar, go to Network & Security > Security Dashboard. ¶ 4. In the Security Hardening widget, click Cluster Lockdown. ¶ 5. From the Your Clusters list, click Lock Down for the required cluster. ¶ 6. Disable remote log on using the Enable Remote Login with Password checkbox. ¶ 7. Delete the SSH key. ¶ To delete the SSH key, click the cross button from the Your Keys list. Your preferences are automatically saved upon configuration. ¶ Vulnerabilities The Vulnerabilities widget displays a list of vulnerabilities (or CVEs) associated with your clusters based on the AOS versions. The Vulnerabilities widget displays vulnerability data for the Prism Central instance and clusters running AOS and AHV only. Click View All Vulnerabilities to view the list of all vulnerabilities and the recommended upgrade path for mitigating the identified vulnerabilities. ¶ Note: Not all the listed CVEs might be resolved when upgraded to a new release. ¶ Starting with Prism Central 2024.1 release, you can update the Vulnerabilities information available on the Security Dashboard. Upgrade the LCM framework to LCM 3.0 release, and then upgrade the Security Dashboard CVE Data using either the connected site or dark site method (web server-based method only). For more information, see Life Cycle Manager Guide. ¶ System Account Passwords View system accounts and their password state. The System Account Passwords widget displays a list of local accounts and the associated password state (default or secure). ¶ You can view the local accounts passwords By Component or By Cluster. Click View all System Account Passwords to change the account passwords using the Centralized Password Management Using System Accounts on page 62 page.

Group: Secure Access
Item: Secure Access Considerations
Guidance: Review the following requirements, limitations, and upgrade behavior before you change the external SSH state on a cluster or activate Support-only Login. ¶ Requirements The following requirements apply to Secure Access on a cluster: ¶ The cluster runs AOS 7.3 or later. The cluster is registered with Prism Central. ¶ Limitations The following limitations apply to Secure Access on a cluster: ¶ Custom scripts and automations that require a bash session on a Controller VM (CVM) must be migrated to Nutanix v4 APIs. For more information, see KB-20212. ¶ Activation of Support-only Login is irreversible. After activation, the token-exchange requirement for full bash access on a CVM cannot be removed, even if external SSH on the cluster is disabled and re-enabled. For the activation procedure, see Activating Support-only Login on a Cluster on page 100. ¶ Upgrade Behavior When you upgrade a cluster to AOS 7.6 or later, the cluster keeps the external SSH state it had before the upgrade. External SSH is disabled after the upgrade only if it was already disabled; if external SSH was enabled or no explicit state was set, it remains enabled after the upgrade.

Item: Managing External SSH Access on a Cluster
Guidance: Enable or disable external SSH access on the Controller VM (CVM) of a managed cluster. ¶ Before you begin ¶ The cluster runs AOS 7.3 or a later version. You have a role that grants permission to update cluster security settings. ¶ About this task To enable or disable external SSH on a cluster, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. Log in to Prism Central. ¶ 2. In the application switcher, select Infrastructure, then go to Hardware > Clusters. ¶ The Clusters page opens on the List tab and shows the clusters that Prism Central manages. ¶ 3. In the cluster list, select the checkbox for the target cluster. ¶ 4. Click More actions. ¶ A menu of additional cluster actions opens. ¶ 5. From the More actions menu, select one of the following options based on the current state of the cluster: ¶ Enable NuService Mode enables external SSH on the CVMs in the cluster so that the admin user can connect over SSH. Note: This setting controls whether external SSH is available, not the type of shell. When the admin user connects, the user lands in the NuService menu, a restricted shell that exposes a curated set of administrative actions, rather than an open bash session. ¶ Disable NuService Mode disables external SSH on the CVMs in the cluster. ¶ 6. In the confirmation dialog box, click Enable NuService Mode or Disable NuService Mode to match the option that you selected. The confirmation dialog box notes that the change applies to all nodes on the cluster. Prism Central applies the change to all CVMs in the cluster and records the change in the cluster audit log.

Group: Secure Access
Item: NuService Menu
Guidance: The NuService menu is the restricted shell that the admin user enters when external SSH is enabled on a cluster. With direct bash access on the Controller VM (CVM), the admin user can run any command on the cluster. Such commands can disrupt cluster operations or alter cluster state in unintended ways. The NuService menu replaces direct bash access with a restricted, menu-driven command-line interface for administrative workflows on the CVM. With the NuService menu, you limit the admin user to approved actions and gain audit visibility for every menu interaction on the CVM. The NuService menu opens automatically when the admin user logs in over SSH. Each menu option runs a curated workflow on the local CVM or AHV host. From the menu, you can perform the following actions: ¶ Run approved commands on the local CVM or on the local AHV host. ¶ View cluster log files. ¶ Manage local LDAP authentication. ¶ Obtain a bash session on the CVM. For more information, see the following topics: ¶ NuService Menu Options on page 97 ¶ Using the NuService Menu on page 98 ¶ Secure Access Considerations on page 95 ¶ NuService Menu Options The NuService Menu provides options to run approved commands, view logs, launch a bash session, and configure local settings on a Controller VM. The NuService Menu offers the following top-level options. Selecting an option runs the corresponding workflow on the local Controller VM (CVM) and returns you to the menu when the workflow completes. Some options open a sub-menu where you select a specific target or action. ¶ Execute Commands Use Execute Commands to run an approved command on the local CVM or on the local AHV host. Execute Commands opens a sub-menu with the following targets: CVM and AHV. Select CVM to run an approved command on the local CVM. Select AHV to run an approved command on the local AHV host or, depending on the command, on all AHV hosts in the cluster. The interactive shell that opens for either target accepts only commands from a curated allow-list. The list includes Nutanix CLI commands such as acli and ncli, system utilities such as ping, traceroute, and netstat, and file-transfer commands such as scp and rsync. To see the complete list of commands available for the current target, type help at the shell prompt. Any command that is not on the allow-list returns an error message. ¶ Log Viewer Use Log Viewer to browse and search cluster log files on the local CVM. ¶ Log Viewer opens an interactive, read-only file browser. From the browser, you can browse log files by name and search across log contents. Use this option to inspect logs for troubleshooting and diagnostics without leaving the NuService Menu environment. ¶ Launch Admin Shell Use Launch Admin Shell to obtain a bash session on the local CVM. The exact behavior depends on whether Support-only Login is activated on the cluster. When Support-only Login is not activated (the default state of the cluster), Launch Admin Shell opens a bash session on the CVM immediately, with no token exchange. Use this option when the curated commands available through Execute Commands do not cover the administrative work that you need to perform. When Support-only Login is activated on the cluster, Launch Admin Shell starts a token exchange with Nutanix Support. You provide the request token to Nutanix Support through an open case, receive a response token, and enter the response token to open the bash session. A successful verification opens a 72-hour access window on the CVM, during which any subsequent Launch Admin Shell selection skips the token prompt and opens a bash session directly. After the 72-hour window expires, the token exchange is required again for any new bash session. ¶ Configure Settings Use Configure Settings to manage local configuration for the NuService Menu on the CVM. Configure Settings opens a sub-menu with an LDAP option. The LDAP option opens a further sub-menu where you can enable or disable LDAP authentication for the NuService Menu. When LDAP authentication is enabled, the NuService Menu prompts for LDAP credentials before it opens. Enabling LDAP for the NuService Menu requires that LDAP is already configured at the cluster level. Disabling LDAP after it is enabled requires a bash session on the CVM through the Launch Admin Shell option. ¶ Help and Exit Use Help to learn what each menu option does, and use Exit to leave the menu. Help displays a description of each menu option. Exit closes the NuService Menu and ends the SSH session. ¶ Using the NuService Menu Use the NuService Menu to run administrative actions on a Controller VM (CVM) when external SSH is enabled. ¶ Before you begin ¶ External SSH is enabled on the cluster. For more information, see Managing External SSH Access on a Cluster on page 96. ¶ You have the password for the admin user on the CVM. ¶ About this task To use the NuService Menu, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. From a workstation, open an SSH session to a CVM as the admin user: $ ssh admin@cvm_ip_address Replace cvm_ip_address with the IP address of any CVM in the cluster. ¶ 2. Enter the password for the admin user. The NuService Menu opens and lists the available options. ¶ 3. Type the number of the option to run, and press Enter. ¶ 4. (Optional) To return to a previous menu, select the back option in the current sub-menu. ¶ 5. Select Exit to close the NuService Menu. ¶ The SSH session ends. ¶ Running Allowed Commands from the NuService Menu Run an approved Nutanix CLI command, system utility, or file-transfer command on a Controller VM (CVM) or local AHV host. ¶ Before you begin ¶ External SSH is enabled on the cluster. For more information, see Managing External SSH Access on a Cluster on page 96. ¶ You have the password for the admin user on the CVM. ¶ About this task The Execute Commands option in the NuService Menu launches an interactive shell that accepts only commands from a curated allow-list. Use this task when you need to run routine administrative commands on the CVM or the local AHV host without obtaining a bash session. For more information on the allowed commands available on each target, see NuService Menu Options on page 97. To run an approved command from the NuService Menu, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. From a workstation, open an SSH session to the CVM as the admin user: $ ssh admin@cvm_ip_address Replace cvm_ip_address with the IP address of the CVM. ¶ 2. Enter the password for the admin user. The NuService Menu opens. ¶ 3. From the main menu, select Execute Commands. The Execute Commands sub-menu opens. ¶ 4. Select the target for the command. The AHV target supports hypervisor-level diagnostics and management commands: ¶ » To run a command on the local Controller VM, select CVM. » To run a command on the local AHV host, select AHV. An interactive shell prompt opens for the selected target. ¶ 5. (Optional) Type help and press Enter to display the list of allowed commands for the current target. ¶ 6. Type the command and press Enter. The shell runs the command and displays the output. The shell rejects any command that is not on the allow-list and returns an error message. ¶ 7. Type exit and press Enter to return to the main menu.

Group: Secure Access
Item: Support-only Login
Guidance: Support-only Login is an opt-in security control that provides bash access on a cluster through a token exchange with Nutanix Support. ¶ Under default Secure Access, the nutanix user still receives a bash session over SSH and the admin user can still reach bash on the Controller VM (CVM). Support-only Login is an opt-in layer on top of Secure Access that closes these remaining bash paths. After you activate it, no bash session on a CVM can start without a token from Nutanix Support. After activation, bash access for the admin user on a CVM requires a token exchange with Nutanix Support and is granted for a fixed 72-hour window. The nutanix user no longer receives a bash session over SSH. Because external SSH to AHV hosts is disabled by default, AHV hosts remain reachable only through elevation from the admin bash session on the CVM. Activation of Support-only Login is irreversible on the cluster. After activation, the cluster cannot return to the default Secure Access behavior. For more information on the activation procedure, see Activating Support-only Login on a Cluster on page 100. ¶ Activating Support-only Login on a Cluster Activate Support-only Login on a cluster to require a Nutanix Support token exchange for any bash session on a Controller VM (CVM). ¶ Before you begin ¶ External SSH is enabled on the cluster. For more information, see Managing External SSH Access on a Cluster on page 96. ¶ You have reviewed the limitations and defaults for Support-only Login. For more information, see Secure Access Considerations on page 95. ¶ About this task You activate Support-only Login by running the configure_restricted_access command from the Execute Commands option in the NuService Menu. For more information about the behavior that activation introduces on a cluster, see Support-only Login on page 99. ¶ Caution: Activation of Support-only Login is irreversible on the cluster. After you activate Support-only Login, you cannot return to the default Secure Access behavior. ¶ To activate Support-only Login on a cluster, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. From a workstation, open an SSH session to a CVM as the admin user: $ ssh admin@cvm_ip_address Replace cvm_ip_address with the IP address of any CVM in the cluster. ¶ 2. Enter the password for the admin user. The NuService Menu opens. ¶ 3. From the main menu, select Execute Commands. The Execute Commands sub-menu opens. ¶ 4. Select CVM to open the allow-listed shell on the local CVM. ¶ 5. Type configure_restricted_access and press Enter. The CVM displays a description of the change, states that the action cannot be reversed, and prompts you to confirm with the message Type YES to confirm and proceed, or anything else to cancel: ¶ 6. Type YES in uppercase and press Enter to confirm activation. Any other input cancels the operation without activating Support-only Login. The CVM applies the change across all nodes in the cluster, which takes a few seconds, and confirms successful activation. ¶ 7. Close the NuService Menu and end the SSH session. ¶ a. Type exit and press Enter to return to the Execute Commands sub-menu. b. Select Go Back to Main Menu to return to the main menu. c. Select Exit to end the SSH session. Support-only Login is active on the cluster. The admin user obtains a bash session on a CVM only through a Nutanix Support token exchange initiated from the Launch Admin Shell option in the NuService Menu. For the procedure to start a bash session after activation, see Obtaining Temporary Bash Access for a Support Session on page 101. ¶ Obtaining Temporary Bash Access for a Support Session Exchange a one-time token with a Nutanix Support to start a temporary bash session on a Controller VM (CVM). ¶ Before you begin ¶ Support-only Login is activated on the cluster. For more information, see Activating Support-only Login on a Cluster on page 100. ¶ External SSH is enabled on the cluster. For more information, see Managing External SSH Access on a Cluster on page 96. ¶ You have an open Support case with Nutanix Support engaged to perform the work that requires the bash session. ¶ About this task When Support-only Login is activated on a cluster, the admin user obtains a bash session on a CVM only through a token exchange with Nutanix Support. After a successful token exchange, the CVM opens a 72-hour access window. During this window, any subsequent Launch Admin Shell selection on the same CVM skips the token prompt and goes straight to a bash session. Use this procedure to complete the token exchange when no 72-hour access window is open on the CVM, or when an open window has expired. The bash session is intended for use only with Nutanix Support. To run approved commands without a bash session, use the Execute Commands option. For more information, see Running Allowed Commands from the NuService Menu on page 99. ¶ Note: If Support-only Login is not activated on the cluster, selecting Launch Admin Shell opens a bash session immediately, without a token exchange. For details about the Launch Admin Shell option, see NuService Menu Options on page 97. ¶ To obtain a bash session through a Nutanix Support token exchange, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. From a workstation, open an SSH session to the CVM as the admin user: $ ssh admin@cvm_ip_address Replace cvm_ip_address with the IP address of the CVM. ¶ 2. Enter the password for the admin user. The NuService Menu opens. ¶ 3. From the main menu, select Launch Admin Shell. The CVM displays a serial ID and a request token, then prompts you for a response token from Nutanix Support. The request token is valid for 30 minutes. ¶ 4. Share the serial ID and request token with the Nutanix Support engineer. Nutanix Support generates the response token and shares it with you. ¶ 5. At the response prompt, enter the response token from Nutanix Support, and press Enter. The CVM verifies the response token, confirms that full access is enabled for the admin user for 72 hours, and starts the bash session. On AHV hosts, Intelligent Platform Management Interface (IPMI) console access is also re-enabled for the duration of the access window.

Item: Updating a KMIP External Key Management Server Using the Prism Central Web Console
Guidance: Update an existing PC-managed KMIP external key management server (KMS) configuration from the Prism Central web console. ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. Log on to the Prism Central web console as an administrator. ¶ 2. Go to Settings > Security > External KMS. ¶ 3. In the table, locate the KMS entry and click the edit (pencil) icon in the Actions column. ¶ 4. Update the name, addresses, CA, or certificates as required, and save the changes. ¶ Note: You cannot change the hostname or IP address, or port of an existing external KMS. To change the hostname or IP address, or port, disassociate all clusters from the external KMS, delete the external KMS configuration from Prism Central, and then add the external KMS again with the new address. ¶ The external KMS configuration is updated. Prism Central automatically propagates the updated configuration to the associated clusters.

Item: Deleting a KMIP External Key Management Server Using the Prism Central Web Console
Guidance: Remove a PC-managed KMIP external key management server (KMS) configuration using the Prism Central web console. ¶ Before you begin Ensure that the KMS entry is no longer in use by any cluster. ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. Group: External Key Management Server on Prism Central > Configuring an External Key Management Server Using the Prism Central Web Console
Item: Configuring a KMIP External Key Management Server Using the CLI
Guidance: Configure an external key management server (KMS) on Prism Central for software data-at-rest encryption. Before you begin Ensure that your environment meets the following requirements: Prism Central version pc.7.5 or later AOS version 7.5 or later Network connectivity and valid certificates between Prism Central and the external KMS Procedure ¶ 1. Log on to the Prism Central VM using SSH. ¶ 2. Create an external KMS instance: ¶ nutanix@PCVM$ mantle_cli kms kmip create --name <KMS Name> --ca_name <CA_Name> -- ca_cert_path <Path to CA certificate> --client_cert_path <Path to client certificate> ¶ -private_key_path <Path to private key file> --ip_port_vec <Comma-separated list of KMS IP address:port pairs> Replace <KMS Name>, <CA_Name>, <Path to CA certificate>, <Path to client certificate>, <Path to private key file>, <Comma-separated list of KMS IP address:port pairs> with the values for your environment. ¶ Note: You can create only up to two external KMS instances on a Prism Central instance. ¶ 3. Verify that the external KMS is created successfully: ¶ nutanix@PCVM$ mantle_cli kms kmip list The external KMS configuration appears in the output, indicating successful KMS creation. ¶ 4. (Optional) Verify that the changes to KMS configuration propagate fully through the Nutanix environment: nutanix@PCVM$ mantle_ops kms_info The KMS configuration can take up to 10 minutes to propagate. ¶ 5. Note the UUID of the external KMS on Prism Central. ¶ 6. (Optional) Enable software data-at-rest encryption on the target cluster using Prism Central if it is not already enabled. a. Log on to the Prism Central web console as an administrator. b. From the Application Switcher option, select the Infrastructure application. c. Go to Hardware > Clusters and from the List view, select the cluster to encrypt. d. Click Actions and select Enable Data-at-Rest Encryption. e. Select the Encryption Type as Encrypt the entire cluster or Encrypt storage containers. f. Click Save Encryption Type. g. Select the Key Management Server as Native (remote) and click Enable Encryption. ¶ 7. Associate the external KMS with a cluster: a. Log on to the Prism Element cluster using SSH. b. Enable the external KMS configuration for the cluster: nutanix@cvm$ ncli key-management-server change-key-manager-server-type key- manager-server-type=ekm_pc kms-uuids=<kms_uuid> Replace the <kms_uuid> value with the UUID of the external KMS obtained in Step 5 on page 105. The kms-uuids parameter is optional. ¶ If you specify one or more UUIDs, only those UUIDs are associated with the cluster. If you do not specify any UUIDs, all external KMS UUIDs configured in Prism Central are associated with ¶ the cluster. The external KMS configuration is configured in the Prism Central instance and associated with the selected cluster. The cluster now uses the external KMS for software data-at-rest encryption.

Group: External Key Management Server on Prism Central > Configuring an External Key Management Server Using the Prism Central Web Console
Item: Updating a KMIP External Key Management Server Using the CLI
Guidance: Update an existing external key management server (KMS) configuration in Prism Central. ¶ Before you begin Ensure that the Prism Central instance is running version pc.7.5 or later. ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. Log on to the Prism Central VM using SSH. ¶ 2. List all configured KMS entries: ¶ mantle_cli kms kmip list Identify the KMS UUID that you need to update. ¶ 3. Update the external KMS details: mantle_cli kms kmip update --kms_uuid <kms_uuid> ca_cert_path=<Path to CA ¶ certificate> client_cert_path=<Path to client certificate> --private_key_path <Path to private key file> --ip_port_vec <Comma-separated list of KMS IP address:port pairs> Replace <kms_uuid>, <Path to CA certificate>, <Path to client certificate>, and <Comma-separated list of KMS IP address:port pairs> with the updated values based on your environment. ¶ 4. Verify that the changes are applied: mantle_cli kms kmip get --kms_uuid <kms_uuid> The external KMS configuration is updated successfully. Prism Central automatically propagates the new configuration to the registered clusters.

Group: External Key Management Server on Prism Central > Configuring an External Key Management Server Using the Prism Central Web Console
Item: Deleting a KMIP External Key Management Server Using the CLI
Guidance: Remove an external key management server (KMS) configuration from Prism Central. ¶ Before you begin Ensure that your environment meets the following requirements: ¶ Prism Central is running version 7.5 or later. The KMS entry is no longer in use by any cluster. ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. Log on to the Prism Central VM using SSH. ¶ 2. List all registered external KMS configurations: ¶ mantle_cli kms kmip list Identify the KMS UUID that you need to delete. ¶ 3. Item: Configuring Active Directory Authentication in Prism Element
Guidance: Configure Active Directory (AD) as the identity provider in Prism Element to enable AD credential-based login for users. ¶ Before you begin Before you configure AD in Prism Element, consider the following points: ¶ The service account for AD must have full read permissions on the directory service. Users with the User must change password at next logon attribute enabled cannot authenticate to Prism Element. ¶ Ensure that users change their password on a domain workstation before logging into Prism Element. If SSL is enabled on the AD server, ensure that Prism Element's firewall allows access to the appropriate port. Use of the Protected Users group is not supported for Prism Element authentication. For more information, see ¶ Guidance about how to configure protected accounts on Microsoft documentation website. Prism Element supports AD with LDAP v2 on Windows Server 2012 R2, Windows Server 2016, and Windows ¶ Server 2019. ¶ Important: Prism Element does not support insecure SSLv2 and SSLv3 ciphers. To prevent the SSL fallback situation and being denied access to Prism Element, configure the following settings in your browser: ¶ Disable SSLv2 and SSLv3 Enable TLS ¶ About this task To configure AD in Prism Element, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. Log in to Prism Element web console as an administrator. ¶ 2. From the main menu, click the gear icon. ¶ 3. On the left navigation bar, select Authentication. ¶ 4. Select the Authentication Types tab and select Directory Service checkbox. ¶ 5. Select the Directory List tab. ¶ 6. Click + New Directory and enter the following information: ¶ Directory Type: From the dropdown list, select Active Directory. Name: Enter a name to identify the directory service on Prism Element. Domain: Enter the domain or sub-domain of the directory service. ¶ For example nutanix.com Directory URL: Enter the URL address of the directory in ldap://host:ldap_port_num format. ¶ host: The host value is either the IP address or fully qualified domain name. ldap_port_num: The default LDAP port number is 389. Nutanix also supports ports 636 for LDAPS, 3268 and 3269 for LDAP/S global catalog servers. Examples: ¶ Default LDAP (Port 389), when the configuration is single domain, single forest, and not using SSL: ldap://ldap.example.com or ldap://10.1.4.111:389 ¶ LDAPS (Port 636), when the configuration is single domain, single forest, and using SSL: ldaps://ldap.example.com or ldaps://10.1.4.111:636 LDAPS requires that all AD Domain Controllers have properly installed SSL certificates. ¶ LDAP/S Global Catalog non-SSL (Port 3268), when the configuration is multiple domain, single forest, and not using SSL: ldap://globalcatalog.example.com:3268 or ldap://10.1.4.111:3268 ¶ LDAP/S Global Catalog SSL/TLS encrypted (Port 3269), when the configuration is multiple domain, single forest, and using SSL: ldaps://globalcatalog.example.com:3269 or ldaps://10.1.4.111:3269 ¶ When the directory URL is set to the domain FQDN, LDAP authentication can fail if any directory server becomes unavailable. For high availability (HA), configure an LDAP HA cluster and specify the cluster virtual IP (VIP) address in the directory URL instead of the domain FQDN. For more information, see KB-12568. When constructing your LDAP/S URL to use a global catalog server, ensure that the domain control IP address or name belongs to a global catalog server within the domain that you are configuring. Otherwise, queries over port 3268 or 3269 might fail. When querying the global catalog, the users sAMAccountName field must be unique across the Active Directory (AD) forest. If sAMAccountName field is not unique across subdomains, authentication might fail intermittently or consistently. Cross-forest trust between multiple AD forests is not supported. LDAPS support does not require custom certificates or certificate trust import. For the complete list of required ports, see Port Reference. Search Type: From the dropdown list, select either Non Recursive (Default) or Recursive. When users are present in the first level group, select Non Recursive (Default). When you have multi-level group assignments, select Recursive. A recursive search performs a multi-level or nested search during authentication, which might cause slowness. If you experience slowness, select Non- Recursive (Default). Service Account Username: Enter the service account user name in user_name@domain.com format. ¶ Note: A service account is created to run only a particular service or application with the credentials specified for the account. According to the requirement of the service or application, the administrator can limit access to the service account. The service account is under the Managed Service Accounts in the AD server. An application or service uses the service account to interact with the operating system. Service Account Password: Enter the service account password. Note: Be sure to update the service account credentials if the password changes or you use a different service account. ¶ 7. Click Save.

For example cn=username, dc=nutanix, dc=com ¶ Note: A service account is created to run only a particular service or application with the credentials specified for the account. The service account is under the Managed Service Accounts in the OpenLDAP server. Click Save.

Group: Security Management Using Prism Element > Authentication in Prism Element
Item: Common Access Card Authentication with Client Chain Certificate in Prism Element
Guidance: Prism Element uses client chain certificate authentication to enable the Common Access Card (CAC) login. Client chain certificate authentication is a certificate-based authentication mechanism where the user is prompted to select a certificate for login instead of a password. Client chain certificate authentication provides enhanced security by requiring users to present a digital certificate instead of a password, reducing the risk of password-based attacks. In a one-way authentication process, Prism Element presents a certificate, and the user's browser verifies it. When the client chain certificate authentication is enabled, the process becomes a two-way authentication. During authentication, Prism Element also verifies the user's identity with a valid digital certificate to ensure that only authorized users can access the cluster. A user must provide a valid certificate when accessing Prism Element. Client chain certificate authentication has the following workflow: ¶ Certificate Installation: A user installs the certificate on their local machine. ¶ Note: The Certificate Authority (CA) must be the same for both the client chain certificate and the certificate on the local machine. ¶ Certificate Presentation and Chain Verification: When the user accesses Prism Element, the system prompts them to select their CAC certificate. Prism Element verifies the presented certificate against its trusted CA chain. The chain establishes trust by linking the client certificate to a trusted root CA. This chain verification step confirms the certificate's validity. ¶ EDIPI Extraction and Account Verification: Prism Element extracts the Electronically Data Interchange Personal Identifier (EDIPI) from the validated CAC certificate. It then queries Active Directory (AD) to verify that the user has a valid and active account associated with this EDIPI. ¶ Authentication Method Selection: Prism Element supports both certificate-based and basic authentication. When a certificate is present, the system prioritizes certificate-based authentication for the login. If a certificate is not present, the system uses basic authentication. ¶ Login: Prism Element logs in the user based on their validated certificate and verified Active Directory account. ¶ Before you configure the CAC, consider the following points: ¶ Prism Element supports AD as directory service for CAC. OpenLDAP is not supported. When you enable CAC authentication, Prism Element disables all other directory services and local user login. ¶ Only the local admin user login is permitted in this case. When you authenticate Prism Element with client chain certificate, the Subject name field must be present. ¶ The subject name should match the UserPrincipalName (UPN) in the AD. The UPN is a username with domain address. For example user1@nutanix.com. If you map a Prism role to a CAC user and not to an AD group or organizational unit to which the user belongs, specify the EDIPI UPN or UPN of that user in the role mapping. A user who presents a CAC with a valid certificate is mapped to a role and taken directly to the web console home page. The web console login page is not displayed. By default, users with an admin role can log in to the Prism Element web console using CAC authentication. For other LDAP user roles, ensure the correct role mappings or role assignments are configured to enable CAC authentication. Client chain certificate must be PEM encoded. If you have logged in to Prism Element by using CAC authentication, to successfully log out of Prism Element, close the browser after you click Log Out.

Item: Emergency Local Account Usage
Guidance: Use the admin account as a local emergency account to ensure access when external services are unavailable. The admin account ensures that both the Prism Element web console and the Controller VM are available when the external services such as Active Directory is unavailable. For all the external authentication, you must configure the cluster to use an external IAM service such as Active Directory. You must create service accounts in the IAM and the accounts must have access grants to the cluster through Prism Element web console user account management configuration for authentication. ¶ Note: The local emergency account usage does not support any external access mechanisms, specifically for the external application authentication or external REST API authentication.

Group: Security Management Using Prism Element > Authentication Best Practices
Item: Modifying the Default CVM Password
Guidance: Change the default Controller VM (CVM) password for nutanix user account by adhering to the password complexity requirements. ¶ Before you begin Before you modify the default CVM password, consider the following points: ¶ Changing the password on one of the CVM is applied to all CVMs in the cluster. Nutanix recommends using the admin user account as the emergency administrative account. Console and SSH direct login are disabled for the root account. ¶ About this task To modify the default CVM password, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. SSH into any of the Controller VMs (CVMs) as a nutanix user: $ ssh nutanix@cvm_ip_address ¶ 2. Change the nutanix user account password: nutanix@cvm$ sudo passwd nutanix ¶ 3. Enter your new password in the command output: Changing password for nutanix. New password: Retype new password: passwd: all authentication tokens updated successfully. Ensure that your password meets the following requirements: ¶ At least eight characters long At least one lowercase letter At least one uppercase letter At least one digit At least one special character (allowed special characters are: "#$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>@[]^_`{|}~!\ ) At least four characters different from the old password Must not be among the last five passwords Must not have more than two consecutive occurrences of a character Must contain at least one character from each of the following four character classes: uppercase letters, ¶ lowercase letters, digits, and special characters Must not contain the words "nutanix", "ntnx", "password", or any simple dictionary words. ¶ Note: Ensure that you preserve the updated nutanix user password. The local authentication (PAM) module requires the previous password of the nutanix user to successfully start the password reset process.

Group: Security Management Using Prism Element > SSL Certificate Management in Prism Element
Item: Generating a Self-signed SSL Certificate with Subject Alternative Name
Guidance: Generate a self-signed SSL certificate with Subject Alternative Name (SAN) using OpenSSL to secure Prism Element. Before you begin The certificate import process validates that the key and certificate pair uses the correct signature algorithm to ¶ comply with NIST SP800-131a and RFC 6460 (NSA Suite B) standards. Use the correct key types, sizes, curves, and signature algorithms. For more information, see Supported Key Configurations for SSL Certificates on page 142. Nutanix recommends including a DNS name for all CVMs in the self-signed SSL certificate using the SAN extension to avoid SSL certificate errors when accessing a CVM through its DNS name instead of the shared cluster IP address. About this task To generate a self-signed SSL certificate with SAN, follow these steps: Procedure ¶ 1. SSH into any of the Controller VMs (CVMs) as a nutanix user: $ ssh nutanix@cvm_ip_address ¶ 2. Generate a private key: RSA private key with a bit length of 2048: ¶ nutanix@cvm$ openssl genrsa -out my_key_name.key 2048 RSA private key with a bit length of 4096: ¶ nutanix@cvm$ openssl genrsa -out my_key_name.key 4096 ECDSA private key using the prime256v1 curve: ¶ nutanix@cvm$ openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -out my_key_name.pem Important: While you are generating the private key, ensure that the private key is not password protected. ¶ 3. Generate the Certificate Signing Request (CSR): ¶ For RSA 2048 and RSA 4096 private keys: nutanix@cvm$ openssl req -new -nodes -key my_key_name.key -signature_algorithm - out my_csr_name.csr signature_algorithm: Specify sha256 or sha384 or sha512. For example, to generate a CSR for RSA 2048 private key using SHA-256 signature algorithm: nutanix@cvm$ openssl req -new -nodes -key my_key_name.key -sha256 -out my_csr_name.csr ¶ For ECDSA 256 private key: ¶ nutanix@cvm$ openssl req -new -nodes -key my_key_name.pem -sha256 -out my_csr_name.csr ¶ For example, to generate a CSR for ECDSA 256 private key using SHA-256 signature algorithm: ¶ nutanix@cvm$ openssl req -new -nodes -key my_key_name.pem -sha256 -out my_csr_name.csr ¶ 4. Enter the information in the command output to incorporate into your certificate request: ¶ You are about to be asked to enter information that will be incorporated into your certificate request. What you are about to enter is what is called a Distinguished Name or a DN. There are quite a few fields but you can leave some blank For some fields there will be a default value, If you enter '.', the field will be left blank. ---- Country Name (2 letter code) []:# Enter the 2 letter country code State or Province Name (full name) []:# Enter the full name of the state or province Locality Name (eg, city) []:# Enter the name of the city or locality Organization Name (eg, company) []: # Enter the legal name of your organization or ¶ company Organizational Unit Name (eg, section) []: # Enter the department or business unit Common Name (eg, fully qualified host name) []:# Enter the fully qualified domain ¶ name (FQDN) of the server Email Address []:# Enter a valid email address Please enter the following 'extra' attributes to be sent with your certificate request A challenge password []: # (Optional) Enter your password ¶ 5. Create a configuration file in your home directory with your preferred text editor named san.cnf that contains the following text: ¶ [req] distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name req_extensions = v3_req ¶ [req_distinguished_name] keyEncipherment [v3_req] basicConstraints = CA:FALSE keyUsage = nonRepudiation, digitalSignature, subjectAltName = @alt_names ¶ [alt_names] DNS.0 = example1.domain.com # Primary domain or fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of ¶ the server DNS.1 = example2.domain.com # Secondary domain or alias for the server DNS.2 = example3.domain.com # Additional domain name that should be trusted ¶ DNS.3 = *.domain.com # Wildcard entry to match any subdomain under domain.com IP.0 = x.x.x.x # IP address of the CVM IP.1 = y.y.y.y # Additional IP address of the CVM ¶ [alt_names] ¶ Specify your DNS and IP addresses. If you have a range of hosts, use wildcards (*) to match any subdomain of the domain name. ¶ 6. Generate a self-signed certificate: nutanix@cvm$ openssl x509 -req -days number_of_days -in my_csr_name.csr -signkey my_key_name.key -out my_crt_name.crt -signature_algorithm -extensions v3_req - extfile san.cnf number_of_days: Specify the number of days until a newly generated certificate expires. signature_algorithm: Specify sha256, sha384, or sha512. Ensure that you use the same signature algorithm that was used to generate the CSR. Example: nutanix@cvm$ openssl x509 -req -days 1460 -in my_csr_name.csr -signkey my_key_name.key -out my_crt_name.crt -sha256 -extensions v3_req -extfile san.cnf ¶ 7. Copy my_key_name.key and my_crt_name.crt from the CVM to your local machine: nutanix@cvm$ scp my_key_name.key my_crt_name.crt username@local-machine:/ local_file_path/ ¶ 8. Log out of the CVM. ¶ What to do next After generating the self-signed certificate with a private key, follow the procedure described in Importing a Self-Signed SSL Certificate in Prism Element on page 138 to replace the default certificate with your self-signed SSL certificate. The following table lists certificate components and its corresponding file type to choose when SSL certificate window prompts: ¶ my_key_name.key Certificate Components my_crt_name.crt Private Key my_crt_name.crt Public Certificate CA Certificate/Chain

Item: Generating a Certificate Signing Request with Subject Alternative Name for Submission to Certificate Authority
Guidance: Generate a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) with Subject Alternative Name (SAN) using OpenSSL for Certificate Authority (CA) submission. ¶ Before you begin ¶ The certificate import process validates that the key and certificate pair uses the correct signature algorithm to comply with NIST SP800-131a and RFC 6460 (NSA Suite B) standards. Use the correct key types, sizes, curves, and signature algorithms. For more information, see Supported Key Configurations for SSL Certificates on page 142. ¶ Nutanix recommends including a DNS name for all CVMs in the CSR using the SAN extension to avoid SSL certificate errors when accessing a CVM through its DNS name instead of the shared cluster IP address. ¶ About this task To generate a CSR with SAN, follow these steps: ¶ Procedure ¶ 1. SSH into any of the Controller VMs (CVMs) as a nutanix user: $ ssh nutanix@cvm_ip_address ¶ 2. Create a configuration file in your home directory with your preferred text editor named ssl.cnf that contains the following text: [req] distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name req_extensions = v3_req prompt = no ¶ [req_distinguished_name] countryName = # Country Name (2 letter code) stateOrProvinceName = # State or Province Name (full name) localityName = # Locality Name (eg, city) organizationName = # Organization Name (eg, company) organizationalUnitName = # Organizational Unit Name (eg, BU) commonName = # Common Name (e.g. server FQDN or YOUR name) emailAddress = # Email Address ¶ [v3_req] subjectAltName = @alt_names ¶ [alt_names] DNS.0 = example1.domain.com # Primary domain or fully qualified domain name (FQDN) of ¶ the server DNS.1 = example2.domain.com # Secondary domain or alias for the server DNS.2 = example3.domain.com # Additional domain name that should be trusted DNS.3 = *.domain.com # Wildcard entry to match any subdomain under domain.com IP.0 = x.x.x.x # IP address of the CVM IP.1 = y.y.y.y # Additional IP address of the CVM [alt_names] - Specify your DNS and IP addresses. If you have a range of hosts, use wildcards (*) to match any subdomain of the domain name. ¶ 3. Generate a private key: ¶ RSA private key with a bit length of 2048: nutanix@cvm$ openssl genrsa -out my_key_name.key 2048 ¶ RSA private key with a bit length of 4096: nutanix@cvm$ openssl genrsa -out my_key_name.key 4096 ¶ ECDSA private key using the prime256v1 curve: nutanix@cvm$ openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -out my_key_name.pem ¶ Important: While you are generating the private key, ensure that the private key is not password protected. ¶ 4. Generate a CSR: ¶ For RSA 2048 and RSA 4096 private keys: nutanix@cvm$ openssl req -new -nodes -key my_key_name.key -signature_algorithm - out my_csr_name.csr -config ssl.cnf signature_algorithm: Specify sha256 or sha384 or sha512. For example, to generate a CSR for RSA 2048 private key using SHA-256 signature algorithm: nutanix@cvm$ openssl req -new -nodes -key my_key_name.key -sha256 -out my_csr_name.csr -config ssl.cnf ¶ For ECDSA 256 private key: nutanix@cvm$ openssl req -new -nodes -key my_key_name.pem -sha256 -out my_csr_name.csr -config ssl.cnf For example, to generate a CSR for ECDSA 256 private key using SHA-256 signature algorithm: nutanix@cvm$ openssl req -new -nodes -key my_key_name.pem -sha256 -out my_csr_name.csr -config ssl.cnf ¶ 5. Copy my_key_name.key and my_crt_name.csr from the CVM to your local machine: nutanix@cvm$ scp my_key_name.key my_csr_name.csr username@local-machine:/ local_file_path/ ¶ 6. Log out of the CVM. ¶ 7. Send your CSR file to the Certificate Authority (CA) of your choice. ¶ After receiving your CSR, the CA sends the following files: ¶ CA signed public certificate CA's public certificate Root CA public certificate (if the CA is intermediate) The issuing CA validates the public certificate. If the issuing CA is intermediate, the root CA validates the issuing CA certificate. The system validates the certificate chain to establish trust. ¶ 8. Download all the certificate files received from CA to the local file directory. ¶ 9. (Optional) If the CA chain certificate provided by the certificate authority is not in a single file, run the following command to concatenate the list of CA certificates into a chain file: $ cat intermediateCAcert.crt rootCAcert.crt > ca_chain_certs.crt Start the chain with the signer's certificate and end it with the root CA certificate. Ensure that the chain file only has the root and intermediate certificates. Prism Element fails to import the chain file if it contains public or private certificates. ¶ What to do next Follow Importing a Self-Signed SSL Certificate in Prism Element on page 138 section to replace the default certificate with a CA signed certificate. The following table lists certificate components and its corresponding file type to choose when SSL certificate window prompts: ¶ my_key_name.key Certificate Components ca_signed_public_cert.cer Private Key ca_public_cert.crt or ca_chain_certs.crt Public Certificate CA Certificate/Chain

Group: Security Management Using Prism Element > SSL Certificate Management in Prism Element
Item: Verifying the Certificate Generation Request
Guidance: Run the following commands to verify the certificate generation request. ¶ Verify that the CA certificate chain is valid: nutanix@cvm$ openssl verify -CAfile ca_chain_certs.crt myPublicCert.cer Example output: myPublicCert.cer: OK ¶ Verify the private key and signature algorithm details: ¶ nutanix@cvm$ openssl x509 -in my_cert_name.crt -text -noout | grep -i 'rsa\|ecdsa\| Public' ¶ Example output: ¶ Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256 Subject Public Key Info: Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey Public-Key: (256 bit) ¶ Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA256 ¶ Verify that the CA certificate chain uses SHA 256 as the signature algorithm: ¶ nutanix@cvm$ openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile ca_chain_certs.crt | openssl pkcs7 - print_certs -noout -text | grep -Ew '(Subject|Issuer|Signature Algorithm):' | grep - C1 Issuer

Group: Security Management Using Prism Element > SSL Certificate Management in Prism Element
Item: Troubleshooting the Certificate Generation Request
Guidance: The following troubleshooting tips can help you resolve common issues that can occur when generating certificates. ¶ Chain certificate format If your chain certificate file has public or private certificates, it will fail to import in Prism Element web console. Ensure that the chain certificate file only has the root and intermediate certificates. For example, if a public certificate is present in a chain file, you can remove it by opening your chain file in your preferred text editor. Ensure that there are no extra white spaces at the bottom of the file. ¶ DER-encoded certificate issue If the certificate is DER encoded, it fails to import in Prism Element web console. You can resolve the issue by converting it to PEM-encoded ASCII format. ¶ Ensure that the certificate is DER encoded: nutanix@cvm$ openssl x509 -in cert.crt -inform der -text -noout ¶ If the certificate is DER encoded, run the following command to convert the certificate from DER to PEM- encoded ASCII format: nutanix@cvm$ openssl x509 -in certDER.crt -inform der -outform pem -out cert.crt ¶ Certificate format Ensure that all the certificates do not have any extra data (or custom attributes) before the beginning (-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----) or after the end (-----END CERTIFICATE-----) of the block.

Item: Importing a Self-Signed SSL Certificate in Prism Element
Guidance: Import a self-signed SSL certificate into Prism Element. Before you begin Ensure that you generate a self-signed SSL certificate. For information, see Generating a Self-signed SSL Certificate with Subject Alternative Name on page 132. About this task To import a self-signed SSL certificate into Prism Element, follow these steps: Procedure ¶ 1. Log in to Prism Element web console as an administrator. ¶ 2. From the main menu, click the gear icon. ¶ 3. On the left navigation bar, select SSL Certificate. ¶ 4. Click Replace Certificate. ¶ 5. Select Import Key and Certificate and click Next. ¶ 6. On the SSL certificate window, provide the following information: Private Key Type: From the dropdown list, select the appropriate private key type for the self-signed certificate. Note: EC DSA 521 and EC DSA 384 bit private keys are not supported. Private Key: Click Choose file and select the private key. Note: The private key that you import must be unencrypted. Password-protected private keys are not supported. Public Certificate: Click Choose file and select the self-signed certificate corresponding to the private key. CA Certificate/Chain: Click Choose file select the self-signed certificate corresponding to the private key. ¶ The following table lists certificate components and its corresponding file type to choose when SSL certificate window prompts: ¶ Certificate Components File type Private Key my_key_name.key Public Certificate my_crt_name.crt CA Certificate/Chain my_crt_name.crt ¶ 7. Click Import Files. Note: Prism Element stores only one custom SSL certificate. When you upload a new certificate, Prism Element replaces the existing certificate. ¶ After you import the new certificate, the Prism Element web console restarts. If the certificate and credentials are valid, Prism Element uses the new certificate immediately. All open browser sessions becomes invalid until you reload the page and accept the new certificate. If the certificate is invalid due to corrupted file or wrong certificate type, Prism Element discards the new certificate and reverts to the default certificate provided by Nutanix.
